asDecan.p: Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Capricorn, roughly the last ten days of December, and each ten-degree slice of a sign has a planet of its own. Capricorn is cardinal earth, ruled by Saturn, the planet of rules and doing things properly, and its Major, The Devil, is your Sun card. The Two of Pentacles belongs to your exact slice, the opening third, where the sign is at its freshest. Jupiter runs it, the planet of more room, more luck, more faith that it'll all work out, and Jupiter is in fall in Capricorn. It's uncomfortable there and nobody much listens to it, so its generosity comes in sideways, through a clever arrangement or a second job or a joke at the right moment. The Three after yours belongs to Mars and puts its head down, and the Four, the Sun's, holds on. Yours keeps a pair of plans going, like the young man in the picture with the boats riding the swell behind him.

You're the person who says yes to the second thing before the first is finished, and it mostly works, which is why you keep doing it. The Saturday you meant to rest turns into the market in the morning, helping your sister move a couch after lunch, and a quote for a side job at the kitchen table that night. At work you're on the phone to a supplier while answering someone's question about the printer. When the budget comes up short, your first thought is never to cancel anything. It's to shuffle, move this bill to next fortnight, sell the bike, pick up a shift. Saturn in you wants a plan and Jupiter wants a bit of slack in it, so you plan with gaps. Friends look at your calendar and wince. You find it fairly relaxing, to be honest, and it's the week with nothing booked that makes you nervous.

Jupiter in fall means your hope has had to prove itself, and it has. You don't tell a friend who's just lost their job that everything happens for a reason. You sit down with them, look at the numbers, find the six weeks of runway they didn't know they had, and by the end of the night they're laughing about their old manager. Being cheerful and having actually done the maths is a rare combination, and people trust your optimism because they've seen you be gloomy about the right things. You're also good at timing, which gets less credit than it should. You can tell which job can hang in the air another week and which one has to be caught today, and you're usually right without being able to say how you knew.

Keeping two plans alive means you never quite have to pick one. The job you half want and the business you half started. Staying in the city while pricing houses on the coast, for about four years. As long as both are moving nobody can say you chose wrong, including you, and the people waiting on the decision, a partner who'd like to know where you'll be living, get tired of asking. Jupiter being in fall shows up here too. The generosity in you is real, often very, and it goes out to other people as favours and help, and then some part of you keeps a tally you'd be embarrassed to hear read out. Your partner can feel it even though you've never once mentioned it. Spending on yourself is harder still. A bonus arrives and within the hour it's gone on the car loan, and the weekend away gets pushed back again.

When something goes wrong, your first move is to add another ball. Somebody's in hospital and you're organising who visits when, still doing your job from the car park, and you've offered to cover the school pick-ups as well. It looks like coping, and for a few days it is. About a week in, the rhythm goes. You start dropping small things, a bill, a birthday, the thing you promised your kid, and you get sharp about it, with yourself first and then with whoever's nearest. The people around you can't find a gap to help, because every job has already been handed to you, by you. What helps is having one thing taken off you completely, handed over and out of your head, with someone you trust telling you it's gone. Then sleep, and a meal you didn't organise.

A lot of people with this slice grew up with a birthday that got folded into Christmas. One present for both, a cake nobody had room for. It sounds small, but plenty of you learnt early not to ask for a fuss, and you carry that into love. You'll plan the anniversary down to the booking and then feel awkward being the one celebrated. You love by making room. You move a meeting to get to their thing, you rearrange a whole month so they can do the course. Your partner may not see how much shifting went into that, because you make it look easy, and then you're hurt they didn't notice. Tell them what it cost, lightly. And let them plan your birthday properly, on a day nowhere near the twenty-fifth.

Capricorn wants to build something that lasts, and the Jupiter in your slice wants it to grow. What you tend to end up with is a working life in two parts running side by side. The day job and the small business. The steady contract and the thing you do on Thursdays that might turn into something. You're good in roles where the ground keeps moving, operations, logistics, events, running a café, anything with a budget and a deadline and too many people wanting things at once. A tidy, fixed job bores you, and you start inventing extra work. The harder part is that Jupiter's big ideas don't get much of a hearing in Capricorn, and yours often don't either. You get hired for keeping things running, and people forget you had a plan. When you've got one, run a small version of it on the side for a few months and bring the numbers to the meeting.

At twenty this pattern mostly looks like hustle. Two jobs, a course, a band, a relationship fitted into the gaps, and a lot of pride in how much you can carry. Money's often tight and you're quite good at being broke. Through the thirties the load gets real, a mortgage, maybe kids, a parent who needs more, and this is where people with this slice either learn to set things down on purpose or get taught it by a bad year. The ones who learn it tend to find Jupiter gets a bit more room, and some good luck arrives that they don't immediately put to work. By the fifties Capricorn has usually paid off in its slow way, and the second thing you kept going all those years is often the one that turns out to matter. Plenty still have something on the side at sixty, a few days' consulting a month, a stall on Saturdays.

Once a week, on the same evening, write every commitment you're carrying on one page, work and home and the favours you've promised. Then cross one off. It doesn't have to be the biggest. It has to be finished, cancelled or handed to someone, and you tell whoever's affected within a day. If you can't find one to cross off, stick the page on the fridge where your partner or housemate can see it and ask them to pick. Do this for a month and look at how the page changes.
